people.name: adrienne maree brown
people.bio: Writer and facilitator whose Emergent Strategy drew from Octavia Butler to map how movements, communities, and change actually unfold — nonlinear, relational, and alive. Essential reading for anyone building cooperatively.
life_story: Born 1978 in El Paso, Texas. An organiser, writer, and facilitator who spent years working with the Ruckus Society and the Movement Strategy Center before turning to the question of how movements actually change — not in theory, but in the body.

She was literary executor for Octavia E. Butler and co-edited Octavia's Brood (2015), a collection of visionary fiction by movement writers. Her own Emergent Strategy (2017) reframed organising through the lens of complexity, fractals, and biomimicry — how small, adaptive practices scale into systemic change.

Pleasure Activism (2019) and Holding Change (2021) extended the work. She is one of the most widely read voices in contemporary organising precisely because she treats joy, rest, and attention to relationship as political practices, not luxuries.

people.name: Alan Watts
people.bio: The philosopher who brought Eastern wisdom to the West. Thousands of lectures freely available — start anywhere.

people.name: Andreas Antonopoulos
people.bio: Educator and advocate whose Mastering Bitcoin and The Internet of Money books, together with his decades of talks, shaped how a generation understood Bitcoin's moral and technical architecture.
life_story: Born 1972 in London, raised in Greece, educated at University College London. Early career in information security. Came to Bitcoin in 2012 and quickly became its clearest public educator — precisely because he was never a founder, never held a major stake, and therefore had no coin to sell.

Mastering Bitcoin (2014) and The Internet of Money (four volumes, 2016–2019) are still the canonical technical and philosophical introductions to the space. He has given hundreds of talks, most available free on YouTube.

In 2017 the community, learning that he had never enriched himself from his advocacy, crowdfunded him nearly 100 BTC in gratitude. He used a portion of it to continue educating full-time, and remains one of the most credible voices in a field full of incentive-distorted ones.

people.name: Andrew Huberman
people.bio: Stanford neuroscientist whose Huberman Lab podcast translates research into practical tools for focus, sleep, and performance. The clearest bridge between the lab and the body in contemporary neuroscience media.
life_story: Born 1975 in Palo Alto, son of a Stanford physicist. BA, MA, PhD in neurobiology, then a postdoc at Stanford and independent lab work at UCSD. Returned to Stanford Medical School as a tenured professor, where he runs the Huberman Lab studying vision, fear, and neural regeneration.

In early 2021 he launched the Huberman Lab podcast, translating peer-reviewed neuroscience into protocols for sleep, focus, light exposure, breathing, and physical performance. By 2024 it was one of the most-downloaded science podcasts in the world.

His work is not without controversy — he is at once a research scientist and a media figure, a position most academics find uncomfortable. The core contribution is durable: a generation of listeners now knows what morning sunlight does to circadian rhythm.

people.name: Anita Moorjani
people.bio: Author of Dying to Be Me, whose recovery from end-stage cancer after a profound near-death experience became one of the most widely shared first-person accounts of what love and self-acceptance can do.
life_story: Born in Singapore in 1959 to Indian parents, raised in Hong Kong. Trilingual childhood, successful corporate career, a conventional life — until, in her early forties, she was diagnosed with stage-four lymphoma.

Four years of deterioration followed. On 2 February 2006, organs failing, she slipped into a coma. In her account of what happened next she moved into an expanded field of awareness in which she encountered her deceased father, a clear sense of the purpose of her life, and a choice of whether to return. She returned. Within five weeks every tumour in her body was gone; within a few months she was discharged.

Her medical records and physician statements are documented. Dying to Be Me (2012) became a New York Times bestseller. She speaks and writes from California now. The NDE literature is vast, but hers is one of the clearest and most reported cases in the modern record.

people.name: Arizona Wilder
people.bio: Former high priestess and MK-Ultra survivor who conducted Illuminati rituals at the highest levels of global power. Her testimony — first recorded with David Icke in Revelations of a Mother Goddess (1999) — covers shapeshifting bloodlines, Satanic ceremony, and the hidden architecture of control. Unfiltered and unflinching.
people.needs_review: URL is her podcast feed, not a personal site. A canonical URL would be better if available.

people.name: Balaji Srinivasan
people.bio: Technologist, investor, and author of The Network State — the foundational text on starting a new kind of country online before building its physical presence. His work maps the organising principle behind the Sanctuary pillar.
life_story: Born 1980 in Long Island to Indian immigrants — both physicians. Stanford: BS, MS, PhD, and MS in engineering, plus a stint teaching a popular class on statistics and data mining. Co-founded Counsyl (genomics) and then 21.co, which became Earn.com and was acquired by Coinbase in 2018.

Served as Coinbase's first CTO and as a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz. Became one of the most widely cited voices in crypto, longevity, and political futures — in part because he treats them as one field.

In 2022 he self-published The Network State, which argued that a new kind of polity could bootstrap online, build moral consensus, accumulate capital, and then negotiate physical territory. The book has become the organising principle behind a generation of experiments. FRQNCY's Sanctuary pillar is downstream of it.

people.name: Barbara Marciniak
people.bio: Barbara Marciniak has channeled a collective of multidimensional beings from the Pleiades star system since 1988. Her book Bringers of the Dawn is one of the most widely read channeled texts ever published — a dense, demanding transmission on DNA activation, timelines, and the game being played on Earth.

channels.name: The Pleiadians
channels.description: A collective of multidimensional beings from the Pleiades star system. Their transmissions through Barbara Marciniak since 1988 cover DNA activation, timelines, planetary awakening, and the deeper game being played on Earth — demanding, dense, and among the most widely read channeled material published.

life_story: Born in North Carolina. Trained as a teacher. In May 1988, during a trip to Athens and the ancient sites of Crete and Egypt, she began to channel a collective of beings who identified themselves as coming from the Pleiades.

The first book, Bringers of the Dawn (1992), is still one of the densest and most widely read channeled texts ever published — an account of Earth as a living library, a game being played across timelines, and the DNA activation said to be underway during this period of human history.

She has continued publishing and teaching for more than thirty years from her base in North Carolina. Earth, Family of Light, and Path of Empowerment extend the same transmission. Read her critically or read her as scripture; the material has shaped the esoteric conversation for a generation.

people.name: Bill Ryan & Kerry Cassidy
people.bio: Since 2006 they have filmed hundreds of hours of whistleblower testimony — insiders from intelligence, military, finance, and the fringes of science — and built Project Camelot into the internet's most important archive of voices the mainstream will not air.

people.name: Birgit Fischer
people.bio: Austrian medium, healer, and four-time SPIEGEL bestselling author — channels Starseed messages and galactic intelligences. One of the most prominent voices in German-language spiritual media.
people.needs_review: Birgit's source material describes her channels as general ('Starseed messages, galactic intelligences') rather than a single named entity. Left the 'channels' array off for now. If you want to add one or more named channels, I'll add them.

people.name: Bob Lazar
people.bio: The man who brought Area 51 and element 115 (moscovium) to public consciousness decades before its scientific confirmation. Official site.

people.name: Bruce Schneier
people.bio: The world's most respected security technologist. His cryptography work, books, and blog form the clearest voice in the field on how systems fail and how to secure them.
life_story: Born 1963 in New York City. Degrees in physics and computer science, then a long career at the intersection of cryptography, policy, and practice. Designed the Blowfish and Twofish ciphers. Wrote Applied Cryptography (1996), which was, for a decade, how cryptographers learned cryptography.

Has fellowships at Harvard Kennedy School and Harvard Berkman Klein Center. Serves on the boards of EFF and Access Now. Has been called the world's most respected security technologist by The Economist — a label he has done nothing to undermine.

His blog, Schneier on Security, has been running since 2004. His books — Secrets and Lies, Beyond Fear, Data and Goliath, Click Here to Kill Everybody — are required reading for anyone who cares how digital systems actually fail. The voice is patient, precise, and unintimidated by power.

people.name: Carl Sagan
people.bio: The cosmologist, science communicator, and author whose Cosmos series and writing (Pale Blue Dot, The Demon-Haunted World) shaped how a generation understood our place in the universe. Science infused with awe, advocacy for reason delivered with poetry.
life_story: Born 1934 in Brooklyn to a working-class Jewish family. Chicago, Harvard, Cornell — he became the rare scientist who was also a public poet. He served as astronomy's bridge to the general mind for thirty years.

He helped NASA design the plaques on Pioneer 10 and 11 and chaired the committee that assembled the Voyager Golden Record — humanity's message to anyone who might find it. In 1980 his Cosmos PBS series reached 500 million viewers in sixty countries. In 1994 he wrote the Pale Blue Dot passage that is still the most widely shared cosmological prose in English.

He died of pneumonia in December 1996, aged 62, after two years with myelodysplasia. His last book, The Demon-Haunted World, is his warning to the century after him: science is a candle in the dark, and the dark is patient.

people.name: Carlo Rovelli
people.bio: Italian theoretical physicist working at the edges of loop quantum gravity and the philosophy of time. His short books (Seven Brief Lessons on Physics, The Order of Time) are among the most beautiful introductions to modern physics ever written.
life_story: Born 1956 in Verona. A physicist who came of age politically in the 1970s — part of Italy's counterculture, with a police file to show for it — before settling into the most abstract problem he could find: what space and time actually are.

He is one of the founders of loop quantum gravity, an approach that tries to quantise gravity itself, and has spent decades working between Italy, the US, and France at the Centre de Physique Théorique in Marseille.

His Seven Brief Lessons on Physics began as a series of newspaper columns for an Italian weekend paper. Translated into more than forty languages, it sold over a million copies — proof that people still want to read about the universe when it is written beautifully.

people.name: Dale Carnegie
people.bio: Author of How to Win Friends and Influence People — the 1936 text on human relations that has sold over 30 million copies and remains the foundation of nearly every communication-skills book written since.
life_story: Born 1888 on a Missouri farm, one of four children in a poor family. Warrensburg State Teachers College, then a string of jobs — sales, a stint in Nebraska peddling bacon and soap, a failed attempt at acting — before he landed on the thing he was actually good at: teaching public speaking at the YMCA in New York City.

The classes became legendary. He wrote textbooks for them. In 1936, drawing on fifteen years of teaching and the stories his students told, he published How to Win Friends and Influence People. It has sold over thirty million copies and, nearly a century later, still sits on most lists of the most influential books of the twentieth century.
He died in 1955. The institute he founded continues to teach his method on six continents. Almost every communication-skills book written since owes him something.

people.name: Darryl Anka
people.bio: Darryl Anka has channeled Bashar since 1983 — teachings on parallel realities, permission slips, and following your highest excitement.

channels.name: Bashar
channels.description: A multi-dimensional being from a future Earth timeline, channeled by Darryl Anka since 1983. Bashar's teachings center on parallel realities, permission slips, and the practice of following your highest excitement in every moment — one of the most accessible and pragmatic transmissions in contemporary channeling.

people.name: David Hoffman
people.bio: Co-founder of Bankless with Ryan Sean Adams. His clear explanations of Ethereum's economic architecture and long-term thesis have made Bankless the primary education source for the bankless generation.
life_story: Born and raised in North Carolina. Trained in software and crypto economics. Co-founded Bankless with Ryan Sean Adams in 2019 — at first a podcast and newsletter, now one of the most-cited media brands in the Ethereum ecosystem.

Hoffman is the one most likely, on any given episode, to explain why a protocol matters at the level of monetary premium and long-term economic architecture. His framing of ETH as money, as a productive asset, and as the foundation of a parallel financial system, has shaped how a generation of investors thinks about the space.
Bankless has grown into a full media company, an investment DAO, and an education platform. Hoffman's long-form essays remain the clearest writing in the business.

people.name: Deepak Chopra
people.bio: Indian-American physician, teacher, and author whose work across dozens of books has brought yoga, Ayurveda, and consciousness into mainstream Western self-development.

people.name: Dolores Cannon
people.bio: Hypnotherapist, past-life regressionist, and founder of Quantum Healing Hypnosis Technique (QHHT). Across 50 years and tens of thousands of sessions she assembled one of the most coherent bodies of channeled material on Earth — Nostradamus, Jesus, starseeds, the volunteer souls, and the shift into the New Earth. Read her or don't, but you can't study this field without her.
life_story: Born 1931 in St. Louis. A Navy wife who in the late 1960s discovered, alongside her husband Johnny, that regression hypnosis could take subjects into something far stranger than past lives. For the next fifty years she refined her method.

In the late 1970s she developed Quantum Healing Hypnosis Technique (QHHT), a protocol for contacting what she called the Subconscious — a layer of a person that appeared to hold information about past lives, future lives, the body's healing, and the broader structure of reality. She trained thousands of practitioners worldwide.

Across seventeen books — Conversations with Nostradamus, Jesus and the Essenes, The Convoluted Universe, The Three Waves of Volunteers — she assembled one of the most coherent bodies of channeled material ever published by a single researcher. She died in 2014 at 83. QHHT continues.

people.name: Dr. David R. Hawkins
people.bio: Psychiatrist and spiritual teacher who mapped the calibrated levels of human consciousness — from shame at the bottom to enlightenment at the top. His kinesiology research revealed that love and truth calibrate exponentially higher than fear and force. Essential for anyone serious about the mechanics of vibration.
life_story: Born 1927 in Milwaukee. A psychiatrist who ran one of the largest clinical practices in New York for decades, treating everyone from celebrities to lifelong schizophrenics. Co-authored Orthomolecular Psychiatry with Linus Pauling in 1973. Conventional, credentialed, and then something broke open.

In 1995 he published Power vs. Force, introducing the map of consciousness — a logarithmic scale from 20 (shame) to 1000 (enlightenment) calibrated through kinesiology. Whether you accept the methodology or not, the framework itself became one of the clearest vocabularies in modern spiritual work for the difference between force and power.
He wrote eleven more books over the next seventeen years, teaching weekend seminars until the end. He died in 2012 at 85. His students describe him as a man whose presence did most of the work.

people.name: Dr. Joe Dispenza
people.bio: Neuroscientist and meditation teacher whose progressive workshops document measurable physiological and psychological transformation through meditation.

people.name: Eckhart Tolle
people.bio: Author of The Power of Now, whose teaching on present-moment awareness brought non-dual consciousness into mainstream Western spirituality. A living transmission of what Osho and Krishnamurti pointed to.
life_story: Born Ulrich Tolle in 1948 in Lünen, Germany. A difficult childhood between Germany and Spain, then a brilliant academic career — University of London, research scholar at Cambridge — and severe, lifelong depression.

At twenty-nine, in a London flat, he had a sudden and apparently irreversible shift in consciousness. He could not function in the academy afterwards. For two years he mostly sat on park benches. Then, slowly, he began to speak to small groups about what had happened.

The Power of Now (1997) grew out of those talks. A New Earth (2005) became an Oprah Book Club selection and introduced millions to present-moment teaching. He lives in Vancouver. The practice is the same one he described on those benches.

people.name: Edgar Cayce
people.bio: The Sleeping Prophet — 20th-century American psychic whose trance readings produced some of the most extensive bodies of channeled material on Earth: health diagnoses, past lives, Atlantis, Jesus. His Association for Research and Enlightenment holds the archive.

people.name: Eileen McKusick
people.bio: Sound therapist and researcher whose Biofield Tuning method uses tuning forks to map and clear the human biofield. Her evidence-gathering approach treats subtle energy as measurable — unusual, rigorous, and deeply effective in practice.

people.name: Emma Grede
people.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Good American, co-founder of SKIMS, founding partner of Savage X Fenty. First Black woman guest Shark on Shark Tank. Her bet: inclusivity — across sizing, race, and access — is a billion-dollar market, not a compromise. Proof that conscious business and category-leading scale aren't opposed.
life_story: Born 1982 in Plaistow, East London, to a Jamaican seamstress mother who raised her and her three sisters. Left school at sixteen, worked her way up through the fashion and celebrity-events industry, and by her late twenties was running her own talent agency.

In 2016 she co-founded Good American with Khloé Kardashian — a denim brand built around inclusive sizing, which grossed over a million dollars on launch day. Co-founded SKIMS with Kim Kardashian in 2019. Founding partner of Savage X Fenty with Rihanna.

First Black woman to appear as a guest Shark on Shark Tank. Her thesis — that inclusion across race, size, and access is a billion-dollar market rather than a compromise — has been proven out at category-leading scale across three brands. Proof that conscious business and commercial dominance are not opposites.

people.name: Erin Claire Jones
people.bio: Brings Human Design into business, leadership, and teams. Known for making HD practical and applicable to work and relationships. Her newsletter is one of the most-read in the HD space.

people.name: Esther Hicks
people.bio: Channels the non-physical collective known as Abraham since 1985. With her late husband Jerry Hicks she transmitted the teachings to millions — the core source of the modern Law of Attraction tradition. Part of the FRQNCY voice lineage.

channels.name: Abraham
channels.description: A collective of non-physical intelligence channeled through Esther Hicks. The most-published voice in the contemporary Law of Attraction tradition — transmissions on alignment, emotional guidance, and deliberate creation.

life_story: Born 1948 in Coalville, Utah. Married Jerry Hicks, a former Amway salesman and seeker, in 1980. Together they spent the early years of their marriage reading Seth, Napoleon Hill, and Jane Roberts — trying to understand how reality actually responds to thought.

In 1985 Esther began to channel a non-physical collective who introduced themselves as Abraham. For the next twenty-five years she and Jerry held workshops across the US, recording hundreds of sessions that became the source material for the modern Law of Attraction movement. The Secret (2006) drew directly from their work.

Jerry died in 2011. Esther has continued teaching. The material itself — deliberate creation, emotional guidance scale, the idea that feeling is the indicator — is woven deeply into the FRQNCY voice lineage, whatever one makes of the channeling.

people.name: Fritjof Capra
people.bio: Austrian-born physicist whose Tao of Physics (1975) drew the parallels between quantum physics and Eastern mysticism that a generation had been waiting for. His subsequent systems-theory work extends into ecology, biology, and economics.

people.name: George Green
people.bio: Former investment banker and USAF veteran who published the Pleiadian-channeled Handbook for the New Paradigm trilogy — available free online and read by millions. His Project Camelot interviews are essential: a man who moved money at the highest levels, who walked away, and who spent his final decades broadcasting what he knew.
people.needs_review: URL points to a specific interview, not a canonical personal site. Consider replacing if one exists.

people.name: Geshe Michael Roach
people.bio: American-born Tibetan Buddhist monk and businessman whose Diamond Cutter teachings bridge ancient Buddhist wisdom with modern business practice. His work reframes karmic mechanics as the operating principle of sustainable wealth.

people.name: Graham Hancock
people.bio: The author and researcher whose work spans lost civilisations, ancient monuments, consciousness, and the hidden history of humanity.

people.name: Grant Sanderson
people.bio: Creator of 3Blue1Brown — the YouTube channel that has redefined how mathematics is visualised and taught. His animations make linear algebra, calculus, and topology not just clear but beautiful.
life_story: Born 1989 or 1990. Studied mathematics at Stanford, then worked briefly at Khan Academy. In 2015 he started a YouTube channel called 3Blue1Brown — named for the colour pattern of his own eyes — to see whether mathematics could be explained the way he wished it had been explained to him.

The videos became the reference point for a generation of learners: Essence of Calculus, Essence of Linear Algebra, the neural networks series, the series on differential equations. He built his own Python animation library, manim, which is now used by educators worldwide.
He accepts no advertising on his videos, relies on viewer donations, and works alone. The result is quiet but enormous: mathematics on YouTube simply looks different because of him.

people.name: Gurumayi Chidvilasananda
people.bio: Siddha Yoga guru and spiritual successor of Swami Muktananda, leading the Siddha Yoga path since 1982. Her teachings on the inner experience of divinity carry an unbroken living transmission.

people.name: Gwern Branwen
people.bio: Researcher, writer, and early experimenter with long-form serious blogging at gwern.net — covering rationalist psychology, darknet markets, machine learning, and everything in between. A model for rigour and intellectual honesty on the open web.

people.name: Helen Schucman
people.bio: Psychology professor who scribed A Course in Miracles from an inner voice identifying itself as Jesus Christ, between 1965 and 1972. Published anonymously for years, it remains one of the most-read channeled works of the 20th century.

people.name: Hermes Trismegistus
people.bio: Legendary figure — part Greek god, part Egyptian sage — traditionally credited with the Emerald Tablet and the Hermetic Corpus. The source of the phrase 'as above, so below' and the foundation of Western esoteric philosophy.

people.name: James Nestor
people.bio: Science journalist whose book Breath compiled the most comprehensive investigation into how humans breathe — and how most of us are doing it wrong. Changed the conversation on the most basic human practice.
life_story: Born in California in the 1970s. A journalist by trade — Outside, Scientific American, The New York Times — who has spent most of his career writing about the edges of human embodiment: free-diving, underwater whale communication, the extremes of breath.

Deep: Freediving, Renegade Science, and What the Ocean Tells Us About Ourselves (2014) was his first book — an exploration of how far humans can descend into the ocean on a single breath, and what it reveals about our physiology.

Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art (2020) examined the more mundane miracle — that most of us have forgotten how to breathe properly, that mouth-breathing deforms the skull, that nasal and slow breathing rewrite autonomic function. It became a global bestseller and, more importantly, changed what a lot of ordinary people do when they inhale.

people.name: Jenna Zoe
people.bio: The most popular contemporary Human Design educator. Her platform makes the system approachable for a modern audience — courses, readings, and a large community. The gateway for most newcomers.
life_story: British by birth, now based between Los Angeles and London. Came to Human Design in her early twenties after a decade of reading every self-help book she could find and noticing that none of them accounted for the fact that different people seem to be built differently.

She founded My Human Design, one of the most-used contemporary platforms for the system — readings, courses, a substantial app, and a large social media presence. Her particular gift is making a dense and often intimidating body of work feel approachable to someone encountering it for the first time.
She is, for a substantial share of the English-speaking world, the door through which Human Design is first entered. Scholars dig deeper from there; she is where most modern readers begin.

people.name: Jerry Hicks
people.bio: Businessman and Dale Carnegie teacher who, with his wife Esther, brought the Abraham material into the world. Co-author of Ask and It Is Given and the central works of the Abraham-Hicks canon. He passed in 2011; Esther continues the work.

people.name: Joe McMoneagle
people.bio: The most scientifically tested remote viewer in history — over 450 operational intelligence missions for the US government.

people.name: Joshua Fields Millburn
people.bio: Writer and co-founder of The Minimalists with Ryan Nicodemus. Their books, podcast, and Netflix documentaries have shaped how a generation thinks about owning less and living more meaningfully.
life_story: Born 1981 in Dayton, Ohio. By his late twenties he was a six-figure corporate executive at a telecom — and, by his own account, miserable. In 2010, after his mother's death and his own divorce in the same month, he began to systematically give away most of what he owned.

He and his closest friend Ryan Nicodemus started a blog, theminimalists.com, documenting what they learned. They quit their jobs. They toured the country in a used car, speaking at bookstores. The audience grew.

Four books, two Netflix documentaries (Minimalism, 2016; The Minimalists: Less Is Now, 2021), and a long-running podcast later, they are the English-language voice of the movement. The core thesis — that owning less creates room for a meaningful life — has reached tens of millions.

people.name: Karen Curry Parker
people.bio: Reimagined the language of Human Design to be more empowering and less mechanical. Her Quantum Human Design reframes traditional HD language — 'Manifestor' becomes 'Initiator,' etc. Prolific author and teacher.

people.name: Kevin Trudeau
people.bio: Teacher and author whose work on the Law of Attraction (Your Wish Is Your Command) and hidden knowledge (Natural Cures) has reached millions. A controversial figure — honest about his own troubles with the legal system — and one of the most direct voices in contemporary manifestation teaching. Part of the FRQNCY voice lineage.

people.name: Krista Tippett
people.bio: Host of On Being — the Peabody-winning radio show and podcast where the biggest questions (what it means to be human, how we live together, what matters in the end) are asked of poets, scientists, and spiritual teachers. Nobody listens more carefully in contemporary American media.

people.name: Lao Tzu
people.bio: The legendary sage whose Tao Te Ching, composed in ancient China, founded Taoism and gave the world one of its deepest wisdom texts — a guide to flowing with the nature of things. Authorship is traditional; the work is eternal.
life_story: Lao Tzu means 'Old Master.' Tradition places him in China around the 6th century BCE, a record keeper in the royal court of Zhou. Whether he was one man, many, or a composite of sages is one of the oldest open questions in scholarship.

The story is that as the dynasty declined he rode west on a water buffalo to disappear into the mountains. At the border a guard refused to let him pass until he wrote down his teaching. The 81 short chapters that resulted became the Tao Te Ching — the book of the Way and its virtue.
It is the second most translated text in human history, after the Bible. Every generation since has found itself in it.

people.name: Lyn Alden
people.bio: The clearest macro analyst covering Bitcoin as an emerging monetary network. Her long-form research bridges traditional finance and the new monetary paradigm.

people.name: Malcolm Gladwell
people.bio: The New Yorker staff writer and author (Outliers, The Tipping Point, Blink) who defines the contemporary art of finding the story inside the research. A master of narrative non-fiction.

people.name: Manly P. Hall
people.bio: American esoteric scholar whose Secret Teachings of All Ages (1928) attempted to map the entire Western wisdom tradition in one volume. His Philosophical Research Society in Los Angeles remains the home of his lectures and library — one of the great archives of sacred philosophy.

people.name: Marshall Rosenberg
people.bio: The creator of Nonviolent Communication. His work underpins almost all modern conflict resolution.

people.name: Masaru Emoto
people.bio: Japanese researcher whose work with water crystals demonstrated the responsiveness of water to thought, word, and intention. His photographic records changed how millions understand the relationship between consciousness and matter.

people.name: Michael A. Singer
people.bio: Author of The Untethered Soul and The Surrender Experiment — books that map the practice of letting go as a path to the direct experience of consciousness. Founder of the Temple of the Universe meditation community in Florida.

people.name: Michael Pollan
people.bio: The writer who reshaped public conversation around food, agriculture, and — with How to Change Your Mind — psychedelic medicine. Rigorous, readable, and relentlessly curious across every domain he enters.
life_story: Born 1955 on Long Island. A journalist by training, a gardener by obsession. For twenty years he wrote about food, agriculture, and the human relationship to the other species we eat and grow.

The Omnivore's Dilemma (2006) and In Defense of Food (2008) reshaped the public conversation about what's on the American plate. In 2018 he turned to another subject long considered unrespectable — psychedelics — and with How to Change Your Mind did for that field what his earlier work did for food.
He teaches at UC Berkeley and Harvard. His voice is the one American journalism tends to produce at its best: curious, precise, and never afraid to change its mind.

people.name: Napoleon Hill
people.bio: The 20th-century writer whose Think and Grow Rich, drawn from interviews with Carnegie, Edison, and hundreds of other successful figures, remains the most-read success book in history. The source code for most of the self-development literature that followed.
life_story: Born 1883 in a log cabin in Virginia. At twenty-five, as a young journalist, he was sent to interview Andrew Carnegie — then the richest man on earth. The interview lasted three days, at the end of which Carnegie gave him a commission: spend the next twenty years studying the most successful people in America and extract the pattern.

Hill took the assignment. Over the next two decades he interviewed more than five hundred industrialists, inventors, and presidents — Edison, Ford, Rockefeller, Wilson, Roosevelt. In 1937, at the bottom of the Depression, he published Think and Grow Rich.
It has sold over a hundred million copies. Nearly every self-development book written since is downstream of it. He died in 1970, still writing.

people.name: Naval Ravikant
people.bio: Founder of AngelList and a philosopher of wealth, happiness, and leverage. His body of aphorisms and long-form conversations is one of the most-quoted bodies of contemporary thought on building a life of sovereignty and meaning.

people.name: Neville Goddard
people.bio: 20th-century mystic whose teachings on imagination as the creative force — 'imagining creates reality' — form one of the deepest wells of the contemporary manifestation tradition. Part of the FRQNCY voice lineage.
life_story: Born 1905 in Saint Michael, Barbados, the fourth of ten children in a tight-knit Anglican family. At seventeen he sailed to New York to become a stage and film dancer, performing on Broadway and in London through the 1920s and 1930s.

In 1931 a black man named Abdullah, said to be of Ethiopian rabbinical descent, accepted Neville as a student in New York. For five years Abdullah taught him Hebrew, scripture, and Kabbalah, and what Neville came to call the Law — the use of imagination to bring states into being. Neville left dancing in the late 1930s to teach what he had learned.

From 1938 until his death in 1972 he gave thousands of free lectures across the United States, mostly in New York and Los Angeles, and wrote thirteen books. In the late 1950s he reported a series of mystical experiences that shifted his teaching from the Law to what he called the Promise — the inner awakening of God in the believer. He died in West Hollywood at sixty-seven, on the day after his birthday.

people.name: Osho
people.bio: One of the most prolific and radical spiritual teachers of the 20th century. Created hundreds of meditation techniques — including Dynamic Meditation — designed specifically for the modern mind. His 600+ books distil everything from Zen and Tantra to Taoism and Sufism into a single voice of absolute freedom.
life_story: Born Chandra Mohan Jain in Kuchwada, India in 1931. A philosophy student who became a philosophy professor, then a wandering teacher who broke with organised religion of every kind. By the mid-1970s his Pune ashram was the most active spiritual laboratory on earth — thousands of seekers from across the world arrived to try the meditations he kept inventing.

In 1981 he moved the community to a 64,000-acre ranch in Oregon called Rajneeshpuram. What followed is well documented: a visionary experiment that collided with the US legal system, a public scandal, deportation, and a return to India. He died in Pune in 1990 at age 58.

What remains is the work. Over 600 books transcribed from his discourses. Hundreds of meditation techniques — Dynamic, Kundalini, Nadabrahma — built for modern bodies and minds that cannot sit still in the old ways. The controversies belong to history. The transmission is still alive.

people.name: P.T. Barnum
people.bio: American showman, businessman, and civic figure best known for founding what became the Barnum & Bailey Circus — and, later in life, for his 1880 lecture and book The Art of Money Getting, one of the earliest practical wealth-mind texts in the American canon.
life_story: Born 5 July 1810 in Bethel, Connecticut, the eldest son of an innkeeper. From his earliest years Barnum had two convictions that never left him: that the public would pay handsomely to be entertained, and that there was no honour in deceiving them past the moment of the show. The combination made him one of the most controversial and one of the most successful figures of the nineteenth century.

In 1841 he bought Scudder's American Museum in New York and turned it into the most-visited attraction in the United States — a chaotic cathedral of curiosities, lectures, freak shows, dioramas, and theatrical performances that drew forty-one million paid admissions across two decades. He toured General Tom Thumb across Europe (twice meeting Queen Victoria) and brought the Swedish soprano Jenny Lind to America in a marketing campaign so meticulously prepared that the term Lindomania entered the language before she had sung a note.

In his sixties he turned to politics — two terms in the Connecticut legislature, one term as mayor of Bridgeport — and to the writing of his autobiography, which went through more than thirty editions. He died in 1891. The Art of Money Getting, the lecture he gave more than a hundred times in his last decades, is the distilled folk wisdom of a man who watched fortunes made and lost in front of him for fifty years and decided to write down what actually worked.

people.name: Paramhansa Yogananda
people.bio: The master who brought Kriya Yoga to the West, and whose Autobiography of a Yogi remains one of the most influential spiritual autobiographies ever written. Steve Jobs requested it be distributed at his memorial. A living transmission of communion with the Source.
life_story: Born 1893 in Gorakhpur, India. From childhood he was obsessed with finding a guru; at seventeen he met Sri Yukteswar and began the training that would define his life. In 1920 he sailed to the United States to represent India at the International Congress of Religious Liberals in Boston. He never fully returned.

He founded the Self-Realization Fellowship in Los Angeles and spent the next thirty-two years teaching Kriya Yoga to Americans. His Autobiography of a Yogi (1946) is one of the most widely read spiritual books of the twentieth century — Steve Jobs famously asked for it to be given to every attendee at his memorial.

He died on 7 March 1952 in Los Angeles, mid-speech, at a banquet honouring India's ambassador. The mortuary that received his body issued a notarised letter stating that over twenty days, no physical decay was observed. Read it literally or read it symbolically — the teaching he left is the same either way.

people.name: Paul Graham
people.bio: Co-founder of Y Combinator and the essayist whose writings shaped a generation of builders. Clarity of thought in service of making things that matter. Start with any essay — they all lead back to each other.

people.name: Paul Selig
people.bio: Contemporary channel whose transmissions from the Guides — published as a series of dictated books — cover incarnation, the true self, and the coming collective awakening. One of the clearest working channels writing today.

people.name: Peter Drucker
people.bio: The father of modern management. His decades of writing shaped how organisations everywhere think about purpose, the customer, and the knowledge worker. The foundational voice in management theory.

people.name: Peter Wohlleben
people.bio: German forester and author whose Hidden Life of Trees revealed the communication, support, and social life of forests — science written with the wonder of someone who has spent his life among the trees.
life_story: Born 1964 in Bonn. Studied forestry and spent over twenty years as a conventional forester for the state of Rhineland-Palatinate — planting, thinning, harvesting according to the German industrial forestry tradition he was trained in.

Then he started to doubt the method. He began to manage a municipal forest in the Eifel mountains along old-growth principles — no heavy machinery, no clearcutting, individual trees respected. Output stayed high. The forest thrived. People began visiting.

The Hidden Life of Trees (2015), written in the voice of a practitioner not a theorist, translated a generation of mycorrhizal research into public language. The book has sold millions of copies and helped shift how ordinary people walk into a forest.

people.name: Ra Uru Hu
people.bio: Born Alan Robert Krakower, Ra Uru Hu received the Human Design transmission in 1987 on Ibiza. He spent the rest of his life codifying and teaching the system — the founder and original voice of Human Design.
life_story: Born Alan Robert Krakower in 1948 in Montreal. A successful adman, then a media executive — editor of a Montreal magazine, publisher, producer — who in 1983 walked away from all of it and moved to the island of Ibiza.

On the night of 3 January 1987 he reports being overtaken by what he called 'the Voice' — a transmission that continued, uninterrupted, for eight days and nights. What emerged was the Human Design System: a synthesis of the I Ching, the Kabbalah, Vedic chakras, astrology, and quantum physics, laid out as a single coherent map of the energetic architecture of a person.

He spent the next twenty-four years teaching it from Ibiza. The IHDS (International Human Design School) he founded trains analysts worldwide. He died in 2011. Every Human Design reading given today still traces back to those eight days.

people.name: Randall Carlson
people.bio: Researcher and geometrician mapping the cosmic catastrophes that shaped human history — Hancock's key collaborator.

people.name: Rhonda Byrne
people.bio: Author whose 2006 book The Secret brought the Law of Attraction into mainstream culture. Her subsequent works on gratitude, love, and manifestation have sold tens of millions of copies — the gateway text for many first encountering these ideas.

people.name: Richard Dawkins
people.bio: Evolutionary biologist whose Selfish Gene (1976) reshaped how we think about life, cooperation, and altruism. One of the sharpest thinkers of the gene's-eye view of biology.

people.name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
people.bio: Potawatomi botanist whose Braiding Sweetgrass weaves indigenous wisdom with Western botany. A meditation on gratitude, reciprocity, and the grammar of being in right relationship with land and life.
life_story: Born 1953, enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. Trained as a plant ecologist at SUNY and Wisconsin, with a doctorate in 1983. Now Distinguished Teaching Professor at SUNY-ESF and founding director of its Center for Native Peoples and the Environment.

Her first book, Gathering Moss (2003), is a lyrical field science of bryophytes. Her second, Braiding Sweetgrass (2013), is something harder to name — a book about gratitude, reciprocity, and the grammar of the living world, written by a scientist who is also a fluent Potawatomi speaker.
Braiding Sweetgrass spent more than two years on the New York Times bestseller list. It has become, quietly, one of the most influential nature books of the twenty-first century.

people.name: Roger Ebert
people.bio: The film critic who elevated popular movie criticism to literature. His reviews, published from 1967 until his death in 2013, remain the clearest record of what it means to watch a film with full attention and write from inside the experience.

people.name: Rupert Sheldrake
people.bio: Cambridge-trained biologist whose theory of morphic resonance proposes that nature has memory — fields through which pattern and habit propagate. A serious scientist who followed the evidence past the edge of what materialism allows.

people.name: Rupert Spira
people.bio: One of the clearest contemporary teachers of non-dual awareness — his books, videos, and retreats are exceptional.

people.name: Ryan Holiday
people.bio: Modern populariser of Stoic philosophy whose books (The Obstacle Is the Way, Ego Is the Enemy) and Daily Stoic newsletter have brought Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus into the hands of athletes, executives, and seekers.

people.name: Ryan Nicodemus
people.bio: Co-founder of The Minimalists with Joshua Fields Millburn. His 'packing party' experiment — boxing up everything he owned to rediscover what mattered — became a foundational story in the minimalism movement.

people.name: Ryan Sean Adams
people.bio: Co-founder of Bankless with David Hoffman. An ex-banker turned Ethereum advocate, he hosts the leading daily podcast and newsletter on decentralised finance. His conviction-driven long-form interviews shape how a generation thinks about money.

people.name: Sadhguru
people.bio: Yogi, mystic, and founder of the Isha Foundation. His Inner Engineering programme has transmitted classical yoga to millions — direct, uncompromising, and always pointing beyond concept. Part of the living lineage FRQNCY draws from.

people.name: Sai Maa
people.bio: H.H. Sai Maa — spiritual master, humanitarian, and initiator of Shaktipat transmission. Her work bridges Eastern wisdom and Western neuroscience in transformational retreats worldwide.

people.name: Sarah (Medical Intuitive)
people.bio: Certified Medical Intuitive and Quantum Healer with over 20 years of practice. Sarah reads the energetic and soul-level patterns underlying physical illness — tracking the unconscious distortions, unresolved trauma, and soul lessons that manifest in the body. Available on YouTube and @medicalintuitive.sarah on Instagram.
people.needs_review: No last name in source data. Kept 'Sarah (Medical Intuitive)' as the display name for now. Revisit when/if a fuller name surfaces.

people.name: Satoshi Nakamoto
people.bio: The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin. In 2008 an anonymous figure posted a 9-page whitepaper and released the software; in 2011 they vanished, leaving the network to the world. The origin myth of programmable money.
life_story: On 31 October 2008, an anonymous figure posted a nine-page paper titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' to a cryptography mailing list. On 3 January 2009 they mined the first block, embedding a Times headline — 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — into the genesis.

For the next two years Satoshi corresponded with early developers, refined the software, and then, in April 2011, sent a final email: 'I've moved on to other things.' They have not spoken since. The roughly one million BTC mined in those early months has never moved.
Whether Satoshi was one person or many, alive or dead, remains one of the great open questions of the internet age. The protocol runs without them.

people.name: Sean Carroll
people.bio: Theoretical physicist working on quantum mechanics, cosmology, and the foundations of reality. His books (Something Deeply Hidden, The Big Picture) and Mindscape podcast bring the frontiers of physics into clear, demanding prose.

people.name: Sri Swami Satchidananda
people.bio: The yogi who opened Woodstock in 1969 and founded Integral Yoga — a synthesis of yoga's major paths. His commentaries on the Yoga Sutras and the Bhagavad Gita brought the classical texts into lived practice for modern Westerners.

people.name: Steven Greer
people.bio: Former emergency physician who founded The Disclosure Project in 1993 — bringing hundreds of military, intelligence, and government witnesses forward to testify publicly about UFO reality. The landmark 2001 National Press Club event remains the movement's most cited inflection point.

people.name: Sugata Mitra
people.bio: British-Indian education researcher whose Hole in the Wall experiments — placing internet-connected computers in Indian slum walls with no instruction — demonstrated that children can teach themselves almost anything, given access and each other.

people.name: Swami Kriyananda
people.bio: Direct disciple of Paramhansa Yogananda who founded the Ananda communities — living examples of Yogananda's vision of spiritual cooperative living. Author of over 140 books and a lifelong carrier of the Kriya Yoga transmission.

people.name: Swami Muktananda
people.bio: Indian siddha yogi who founded Siddha Yoga and brought the experience of Shaktipat — direct transmission of spiritual energy — to generations of seekers. His Play of Consciousness remains one of the clearest autobiographical accounts of awakening.

people.name: Sylvia Earle
people.bio: The legendary oceanographer known as Her Deepness — former chief scientist of NOAA, founder of Mission Blue, and one of the most visible voices for ocean conservation. Her Hope Spots initiative is building a global network of protected marine areas.

people.name: Thich Nhat Hanh
people.bio: Zen master, peace activist, and the teacher who gave the West its most accessible entry into mindfulness. His presence in a single sentence is a whole practice. One of the definitive voices of the 20th century.

people.name: Three Initiates
people.bio: Pseudonymous authors of The Kybalion (1908), the modern distillation of seven Hermetic principles — mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, gender. Identity unknown. Text foundational.
life_story: The Kybalion was published in Chicago in 1908 by the Yogi Publication Society. On the title page: 'By Three Initiates.' No names, then or since.

The book distils what it calls the seven Hermetic principles — mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, gender — drawn, it claims, from a secret oral tradition descended from Hermes Trismegistus. Scholars have long suspected the primary author was William Walker Atkinson, a prolific early-twentieth-century New Thought writer in Chicago, possibly collaborating with Paul Foster Case or Michael Whitty.

The anonymity was the point. A book that refused to be credited to anyone behaved, in the end, more like scripture than authorship. Whether the principles are ancient or modern, the text is foundational to everything that came after — from New Thought to Law of Attraction to the vibrational language FRQNCY still speaks.

people.name: Viktor Frankl
people.bio: Austrian psychiatrist and Auschwitz survivor whose Man's Search for Meaning gave the 20th century its clearest case for the primacy of meaning in human life. Founder of logotherapy.

people.name: Vitalik Buterin
people.bio: Co-founder of Ethereum and one of the clearest thinkers writing at the intersection of cryptography, economics, and governance. His essays are the primary source for understanding where programmable money is headed.
life_story: Born 1994 in Kolomna, Russia. Emigrated with his family to Canada at six. At seventeen he co-founded Bitcoin Magazine; at nineteen he dropped out of university to build Ethereum, arguing that Bitcoin's scripting language was too narrow for what programmable money could be.

Ethereum launched in July 2015. By the end of the decade it was the settlement layer for most of DeFi, most of NFTs, and most of the experimental economic systems being built online. Buterin remained its public conscience — writing essays on governance, credibility, and public goods that are read as carefully as the protocol's code.

He holds no operational role, draws no salary, and has given away hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of tokens to longevity research and pandemic relief. The rarest kind of founder: the one who tried to make himself unnecessary.

people.name: Walter Isaacson
people.bio: The biographer who brought the inner lives of Einstein, Steve Jobs, Benjamin Franklin, Leonardo da Vinci, and Jennifer Doudna into clear, human-scale prose. Among the most respected biographers writing today.
